in_context.text: Paul is closing the first section of his letter, where he tells Timothy to stop false teachers in Ephesus. He hands Timothy this 'charge' (1:18) and urges him to keep both faith and a good conscience. He warns that some have thrown conscience aside and wrecked their faith, and in the next verse he names two of them.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the writer at the start of the letter.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker and 'own son in the faith,' whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: The 'some' who made shipwreck of their faith. Paul names Hymenaeus and Alexander as examples.

what.text: Timothy is to keep holding two things together: faith and a good conscience. Some people pushed conscience away, and as a result their faith broke apart like a wrecked ship. This echoes 1:5, where the goal of Paul's instruction is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith.

events.text: This happens after Paul left Timothy in Ephesus and went on to Macedonia. False teachers were troubling the church there.

written.text: Traditional view: Paul wrote it about AD 62-64, between his two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110 and think a follower wrote it in Paul's name, while others defend Paul's authorship and the earlier date.

where.text: Timothy was in Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. The letter does not say where Paul wrote from, though he had gone on to Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul wants Timothy to 'war a good warfare' against false teaching. Here he shows what Timothy must guard in himself, and what happens to those who don't.

big_picture.text: A key theme of the letter is that belief and behavior belong together. Here, giving up a good conscience leads straight to the ruin of faith. Paul says the same of church servants in 3:9: 'Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.'

for_readers.text: Faith is not only a set of beliefs. It is kept safe by an honest conscience and right living, and ignoring conscience can sink it.

christians_differ.text: Christians read "made shipwreck" differently. Some see it as proof that real believers can fall away, and link it with Hebrews 6:4-6. Others hold that true believers are kept safe, and read it as the collapse of a faith that was only professed, or as serious damage short of final loss.

why_it_matters.text: The word means to thrust something away from oneself, to reject it. This was not a slow drift. These people deliberately shoved conscience aside.
This is the ordinary word for suffering shipwreck, which Paul also uses of his own wrecks at sea in 2 Corinthians 11:25. Here it is used as a picture of what happened "concerning faith."
It means the inner sense that judges one's own conduct. A 'good conscience' appears in 1:5 and here, which ties right living closely to sound faith.
The word can mean to hold fast. It fits the battle picture of 1:18: Timothy must keep a firm grip on faith and conscience.

takeaway.text: Keep faith and a clear conscience together. Pushing conscience aside can wreck faith itself, as happened to some in Ephesus.

resolved.reason: The lexicon only says the word is used metaphorically of shipwreck regarding faith. Saying faith is 'lost, not merely damaged' takes one side of the interpretive debate that christians_differ itself presents as open.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources

resolved.reason: No cited source says that 'many on both sides' read verse 20's 'may learn' as pointing to possible restoration. The verse states a corrective purpose, but the claim about how interpreters read it is not supported.
